neighbours.label: a plant's defensive substance or structure against herbivores (stinging hairs, toxins, bitter chemicals, milky latex), as opposed to non-defensive plant features in the same frames
fire: Holly protects its leaves from deer with sharp spines along the edges.
Tobacco plants produce nicotine to poison the insects that chew them.
Many euphorbias bleed a milky latex that burns the skin of grazers.
Oak leaves are full of bitter tannins that put caterpillars off.
Cassava roots contain cyanide compounds that must be removed by soaking.
Acacia trees grow long thorns to keep giraffes from browsing.
Foxglove contains toxic glycosides that can kill livestock.
Some grasses store silica in their blades to wear down the teeth of grazers.
quiet: Holly brightens the garden in winter with glossy green leaves.
Tobacco plants produce pink flowers that open in the evening.
Many euphorbias grow well in dry, sunny rock gardens.
Oak leaves turn brown and fall late in the autumn.
Cassava roots are boiled and mashed for the evening meal.
Acacia trees grow tall on the open plains of Kenya.
Foxglove blooms in tall purple spikes in early summer.
Some grasses spread quickly across sandy soil near the coast.
